flawed_step: The statement treats convergence in distribution as if it implied convergence in probability. Convergence in distribution only involves the marginal distribution functions. It says nothing about how X_n and X are coupled on the common probability space.
counterexample: Let Ω = {a, b} with P({a}) = P({b}) = 1/2. Set X(a) = 1 and X(b) = -1, and let X_n = -X for every n, so X_n(a) = -1 and X_n(b) = 1. Both X_n and X take the values ±1 with probability 1/2 each. So F_{X_n}(t) = F_X(t) for all t: 0 for t < -1, 1/2 for -1 ≤ t < 1, and 1 for t ≥ 1. This means F_{X_n}(t) → F_X(t) at every t, so X_n → X in distribution. But |X_n - X| = |−2X| = 2 at every sample point. With eps = 1, P(|X_n - X| > 1) = 1 for all n, which does not tend to 0. So X_n does not converge to X in probability.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. Take X_n = -X, where X is a symmetric ±1 variable. Every X_n has exactly the same distribution as X, so X_n → X in distribution. Yet |X_n - X| = 2 surely, so P(|X_n - X| > 1) = 1 for all n and there is no convergence in probability. The implication does hold when X is almost surely constant, but not in general.
